text: In Mauritius, people and communities engage in the practice of cultural blending, respect, and coexistence while maintaining distinct identities. This behavior aims to preserve cultural heritage and foster peaceful coexistence among various ethnic, religious, and societal groups. Both Mauritians and foreigners reciprocate this behavior by responding with respect and upholding their own cultural identities. The influence of Western, African, and Asian cultures has contributed to the unique cultural landscape, with distinct communities likened to a fruit salad, each maintaining its individual flavor while contributing to the overall diversity. This practice is widely regarded as a normative and harmonious way of life by a significant portion of the sampled population.

In Mauritius and among Mauritian communities, individuals and society exhibit a norm of speaking multiple languages, including Kreol, English, French, Hindi, Urdu, Bhojpuri, and Mandarin, with a preference for French and Creole. This multilingual behavior serves the goal of effective communication and the preservation of cultural identity. It is common for both Mauritian individuals and non-Mauritians to engage in conversations using these languages, actively listening, responding, and participating in the linguistic diversity. The significant presence of Mauritian Creole in this language mix further emphasizes its importance within the cultural context. While not universally practiced, this multilingual communication is regarded as a notable aspect of Mauritian cultural interaction.

In Mauritius and abroad, residents and individuals of Mauritian descent engage in a wide range of activities, from leisure pursuits to business endeavors, with a strong emphasis on upholding traditional gender roles and promoting the island. Their goal is to preserve cultural values, enjoy leisure time, and showcase the beauty of the island. In various relationships, such as family and business, tourists, family members, and individuals from other nations participate in activities and invest in the island. Mauritius, with its diverse cultural heritage and reputation for lower corruption compared to other developing nations, is increasingly recognized as a regional hub for IT, finance, and education. This behavior is widely regarded as a normative practice within the sampled population.

Most people tend to be indirect in most situations. People will often tell you what they think you may want to hear rather than risk hurting feelings or embarrassing someone with the truth. People are proud of their island and may expect you to admit that it’s the closest thing to Paradise , so it’s a good idea to just oblige. Be open and friendly and accept offerings.

An arm’s length of personal space is common for friends and family. For business colleagues and members of the opposite sex this space may be a bit more, but it all depends on how close the relationship is. Female friends often hold hands while walking and touching. It is common for them to pat each other on the back, arms, shoulders, etc. Men often playfully slap each other on the shoulder, especially good friends and family. For business colleagues and members of the opposite sex touching is usually kept to a minimum.
Direct eye contact is acceptable in most situations.

People tend to be punctual in both social and business situations. For example, if invited for lunch to Mauritian home that is called at noon, don’t be surprised to find that people may have already eaten if you are more than 20-30 minutes late. Transportation services tend to run on time for the most part. People do not tend to give their time freely. It’s quite challenging to have people volunteering on weekends for example.

Gender equality has begun to take hold in the last few years. For example, the first lady taxi driver was featured in the news and on the newspapers about 6 years ago. Now jobs such as bus ticket seller (on the bus) which were exclusively male have become quite common for women. Women are expected to achieve academic success at a high level and have jobs that meet those expectations. They tend to be very competitive in this respect.

The Mauritian word for taboo behavior is “sauvaze” (pronounced so vaz). It means savage which refers to a person who would be too loud, a too brazen, or a women seen drinking, dressed inappropriately, smoking, etc.

The legal drinking and smoking age is 18. It does not tend to be that heavily enforced. Sodomy is legally prohibited and punishable by imprisonment. Penalties for the possession, use or trafficking of illegal drugs are severe and convicted offenders can expect prison sentences.
